title: Contentment with little
hook: a full cart that never checks out, and a one-sentence definition of wealth

segments.voice: Yesterday: loving for others, with your own wanting as the ruler. Today, a different kind of being rich.

An online cart, full, never checked out. A closet with the tags still on. A search at three in the morning for something nobody needed at noon. Sometimes the wanting doesn't end when the package arrives; it moves on to the next thing. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, put a definition of wealth into one sentence. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: richness isn't having a great many things; real richness is richness of the soul.
screen: `A CART THAT NEVER CHECKS OUT.` → `THE WANTING MOVES ON.` → `RICHNESS OF THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: The word is qana'ah: contentment, being satisfied with what you've been given. The soul in the hadith is nafs, the same word this path has used for the self that wants and wants. So the hadith moves wealth off the shelf and into the self. Two people can own exactly the same things. One feels poor, because the wanting runs ahead. The other feels rich, because it doesn't. But qana'ah isn't a vow to have nothing. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says, in paraphrase: successful is the one who has submitted, been given enough to live on, and been made content by Allah with what He gave. Enough. Not nothing. A way to train it, also in Muslim, in paraphrase: look at those below you, not at those above you; that way you won't belittle Allah's blessings on you. Look down the ladder, not up. A phone feed tends to run the other way. And a story of someone who missed it. In surah al-Kahf, a man with two rich gardens walks into his own grounds and says he doesn't think any of this will ever perish. His companion asks him, in paraphrase: when you entered your garden, why didn't you say, what Allah wills; there is no strength except in Allah? Ma sha' Allah. You may hear it said over a new baby, a new house, a friend's success. It hands the good thing back to the One who gave it. Qana'ah is being able to stop at enough.
screen: `NAFS: WEALTH MOVES INTO THE SELF.` · `ENOUGH, NOT NOTHING.` · `LOOK DOWN THE LADDER, NOT UP.` · `THE TWO GARDENS: MA SHA' ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you already own and haven't really looked at in a while, a mug, a coat, a window, shoes that still work, and look at it the way you'd look at something just unwrapped. Notice what it does for you every day without asking anything back. If you pray, you can say quietly, ma sha' Allah, or alhamdulillah; if not, just stay with the thing, and with the word enough.
Qana'ah. Contentment: richness of the soul, enough given and enough accepted, without the wanting running ahead. Today's word.
Your line: rich in the soul. Enough, not nothing. That's today, done.

howItsDone: Muslims cultivate qana'ah by thanking Allah for what they have, saying ma sha' Allah over good things, and following the hadith's advice to look at those with less rather than those with more.

trapdoor: what you thought: contentment means not wanting anything.
what it means: qana'ah is stopping at enough: richness of the soul, given enough and made content with it.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 6446's ghina al-nafs beside Muslim 1054's 'given enough': contentment is not poverty but a self that isn't chasing.

chat.says: Does contentment in Islam mean you're supposed to own nothing?
options: No. A hadith praises having enough to live on and being content with it.
Yes. The hadith says the successful one is the one who owns nothing at all.
No, it means getting rich first; after that, you'll feel content.
chat.meaning: Qana'ah is enough, not nothing: the hadith in Sahih Muslim praises one given enough to live on and made content with it.
